newsitem.title: USA: USDA economist -'97 cotton, wheat, rice sowing down.
newsitem.headline: USDA economist -'97 cotton, wheat, rice sowing down.

text.p: U.S. farmers are likely to plant slightly less cotton, wheat and rice than in 1996 while the "market fundamentals look good" for soybeans and feed grains, the Agriculture Department's chief economist said Tuesday.
Economist Keith Collin said U.S. wheat supplies should be adequate in the 1997-98 trading year despite indications of a seven percent drop in winter wheat acreage.
"We can easily do better than one billion" bushels in wheat exports, Collins said, with normal weather and average spring wheat sowings.
The outlook for wheat supplies in 1997-98 was aided, Collins said, by USDA's decision to raise its estimate of 1996-97 end stocks by 34 million bushels to a total of 374 million.
It would partially offset a loss of about 75 million bushels in likely winter wheat producton due to the smaller sowings.
"Market fundamentals look very good" for encouraging feed grain and soybean plantings, Collins said.
"We expect the annual kinds of substitutions with a little less rice, a little less cotton (and) a little less wheat."
Corn acreage could be lose to 80 million acres and soybeans around 64 million acres.

By comparison, corn plantings were 79.5 million acres and soybeans 64.2 million last year. A wet spring prevented farmers from planting as much corn as they wanted. Some fields were switched to oilseeds.
About 75.6 million acres of wheat were planted for 1996 harvest, including 51.9 million of winter wheat. Some 48.2 million were sown for this year, USDA said.
Collins said USDA had expected 50-51 million acres sown.
U.S. wheat output could reach 2.25-2.3 billion this year, which would put total supply at 2.75 billion bushels, adequate for some stockbuilding and export growth, Collins said.
